strengths: Originality/significance: Modeling per-prompt output length as a distribution rather than a point estimate is a useful perspective, and combining censored expectation with CVaR yields a simple scheduling score that could be practically valuable.

Empirical breadth: The paper evaluates online and offline settings, multiple datasets, Llama 8B/70B, six additional model families, and OpenPanGu. TIE consistently improves reported mean and P90 latency and deadline-based completion counts, often substantially.
The system design is concrete: the vLLM implementation, asynchronous prediction, dynamic batching, heap-based scheduling, and starvation decay make the proposal more than a conceptual scoring rule.
The censored log-t expectation and CVaR derivations are supplied, and Table 4 usefully compares log-t against log-normal, expectation-only SEPT, and fixed versus adaptive CVaR weighting.
Presentation is generally clear and polished. The motivation, architecture, scheduler, and experimental results are easy to follow, and the figures and tables are legible.

The paper honestly identifies the substantial data-collection burden of repeated generations. No major research-ethics issue is apparent, although the fairness implications of deprioritizing long requests deserve more attention.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical result does not establish the paper's principal log-t modeling claim. Appendix A effectively replaces the time-varying, trajectory-dependent EOS probabilities with a fixed latent termination rate and assumes that this rate has density f(p)~c p^(alpha-1) near zero. That assumption nearly builds in the resulting power-law mixture tail, is not empirically validated, and does not imply a log-t distribution.

The reported KS evidence is statistically questionable. Distribution parameters are estimated from the same 100 observations on which ordinary KS p-values are computed, so standard KS p-values and the stated p>0.05 pass rates are not calibrated without a parametric bootstrap or an appropriate composite-null correction. The fixed degree of freedom is also selected using average p-value on these data. Discreteness and possible max-token censoring of output lengths are not handled in the fitting analysis.

The evaluation does not isolate the proposed uncertainty-aware score from system-level changes. TIE receives asynchronous, dynamically batched prediction, but the paper describes existing baselines as using synchronous prediction and provides no common-infrastructure comparison. There are likewise no ablations of asynchronous batching, the 3 ms timeout, starvation decay, or the adaptive pressure rule. Consequently, the large end-to-end gains cannot be confidently attributed to distribution modeling or TIE.

Critical workload details are missing: decoding temperature/top-p and max-token settings, request-arrival process, experiment duration and warm-up, random seeds, number of repetitions, variance or confidence intervals, and whether all methods see identical generated jobs. Output-length uncertainty depends directly on these choices, making both the fitted distributions and system results difficult to reproduce.

The online experiments appear heavily overloaded (for example, tens to hundreds of seconds of TTFT at 100 RPS). In this regime averages depend strongly on run horizon and unfinished requests. The paper reports neither stability/queue growth nor completion-conditioned accounting, p99/max latency, per-request slowdown, or starvation/fairness statistics, despite explicitly delaying predicted-long requests.

The offline metrics—time to the first 3,000 completions and number completed within three minutes from 10,000 submitted prompts—intrinsically reward postponing long requests. They do not demonstrate improved total-job makespan or steady-state token throughput. Reporting these quantities simply as throughput overstates the system-level conclusion; full-drain time, tokens/s, and fairness to long jobs are needed.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. TIE uses only 45,000 unique prompts repeated 20 times, while SSJF/LTR use 900,000 prompt-response samples; equating these solely by generation count does not equate semantic coverage or collection cost. Predictor architectures, tuning budgets, held-out splits, and whether the reported R² values are on unseen prompts are also unclear.

The claimed cross-model generalization is promising but mechanistically underexplained because a predictor trained on Llama-3-8B targets is reused for models with different decoding behavior. There is no direct evaluation of predicted distribution calibration, likelihood, quantile coverage, tail recall, or ranking quality on the transferred models to substantiate the explanation offered for the scheduling gains.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: several training details are deferred to unspecified code, and no artifact or complete configuration is identified in the manuscript. Monte Carlo estimation with 10,000 draws per request is also underspecified regarding seed reuse, numerical stability, and whether its cost is included in the 4.26 ms figure.

The limitations and impact discussions are too narrow. Beyond data collection, the paper should acknowledge dependence on decoding configuration, questionable fit-test calibration, overload/fairness tradeoffs, and the possibility that prompts eliciting long answers—or user groups correlated with them—receive systematically worse service. Overall, the idea has clear merit, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps currently outweigh it.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a practically important systems problem—head-of-line blocking in LLM serving—and evaluates both interactive and offline workloads.
Originality: Predicting a prompt-conditional output-length distribution and incorporating tail risk through a CVaR-based scheduling score is a useful extension of point-estimate SJF methods.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers several datasets, model sizes, and architectures, including MoE models. The expectation-only, fixed-risk, adaptive-risk, and alternative-distribution ablations are informative.

Presentation: The main pipeline is understandable, the paper is generally well organized, and the authors explicitly acknowledge the substantial cost of collecting repeated generations for each training prompt.

Engineering: Asynchronous prediction, dynamic batching, heap-based scheduling, and waiting-time decay form a plausible deployable design; the reported predictor/scheduler overhead is small relative to latency under the evaluated high-load condition.
weaknesses: Soundness—theoretical claim: Theorem 3.2 does not establish that ordinary autoregressive LLM decoding produces heavy-tailed lengths. The crucial step from time- and history-dependent EOS probabilities p_t to a single fixed latent termination rate per trajectory (Eq. 17) is an additional strong mixture-of-geometric assumption, not a consequence of Assumption 3.1 or the preceding lemma. Indeed, the appendix informally motivates this by saying a trajectory's “type” is determined early, rather than deriving or empirically validating it. Thus the advertised theoretical explanation is largely assumption-driven.

Soundness—distribution testing: The reported KS p-values and “pass rates” are not statistically calibrated because distribution parameters are fitted on the same 100 observations used for each KS test. A parametric-bootstrap/Lilliefors-style calibration is needed. Selecting ν using average in-sample KS p-values adds further selection bias, and 100 samples per prompt provide weak evidence about extreme tails. Figure 7 itself shows that σ remains materially less stable than μ at the chosen 20-repetition training setting.

Soundness—causal attribution: TIE is evaluated as a bundle comprising a different predictor/target, CVaR scoring, adaptive queue-pressure weighting, starvation decay, asynchronous prediction, and dynamic batching. The paper does not establish that SSJF and LTR receive the same asynchronous batching and queue implementation, nor does it report their prediction/scheduling overhead. Consequently, the very large end-to-end gains cannot be confidently attributed to uncertainty-aware distribution modeling. Table 4 only partially addresses this confounding.

Evaluation methodology is underspecified: The manuscript omits essential details such as arrival-process construction, run duration and warm-up, decoding temperature/top-p and random seeds, max-token settings, prompt/test sampling, number of independent trials, variance or confidence intervals, and predictor train/validation/test splits. It is unclear whether LMSYS evaluation prompts overlap the first 45K prompts used to train TIE. No code or sufficiently complete implementation specification is included; referring to “details ... in our code” is inadequate in the submitted manuscript. These omissions materially limit reproducibility. Significance of the offline result is overstated: “throughput within 3 min” and time to the first 3K completions measure transient completion ordering after submitting 10K jobs. An SJF-like scheduler can improve these quantities simply by postponing long requests without increasing steady-state service capacity or total-job makespan. Calling the resulting 1.42× improvement a throughput gain is therefore misleading unless total completion time, steady-state admitted throughput, unfinished work, and fairness are also reported.

The online experiments operate in extreme overload—average TTFTs range from tens to hundreds of seconds—and emphasize mean and P90 metrics that naturally benefit from sacrificing long requests. There is no SLO goodput, P99/max latency, per-length-class latency, slowdown, or fairness analysis. The proposed starvation decay is not experimentally evaluated, so the paper does not demonstrate acceptable treatment of long-request users.

The distribution-family comparison is incomplete. Log-t has an exceptionally heavy tail with no uncensored mean, making results highly dependent on max_tokens censoring, yet sensitivity to max_tokens is absent. Comparison against flexible empirical quantiles, survival models, mixture models, heteroscedastic quantile regression, or direct risk-score/ranking prediction would be needed to show that log-t distribution estimation itself is necessary.

Presentation contains unsupported interpretations. For example, tighter completion-time/output-length heatmaps are treated as evidence of more accurate output-length characterization, but this pattern is itself induced by the scheduler and is not a prediction-accuracy evaluation. Only aggregate R² for μ and σ is given; calibration, tail coverage, quantile loss, ranking accuracy, and held-out likelihood are missing.

Limitations and ethics: The limitation section discusses repeated-generation cost but omits the central risks of model misspecification, workload drift, overloaded-regime evaluation, and systematically delaying verbose or complex task classes. The generic impact statement does not analyze fairness or denial-of-service implications of priority scheduling. These are not necessarily prohibitive ethical concerns, but they require measurement and discussion.

Overall: The core idea is promising, but invalidly calibrated distribution evidence, an assumption-driven theoretical claim, substantial experimental confounding, missing reproducibility details, and throughput/fairness metrics that favor SJF by construction prevent the central claims from being considered reliable. Major redesign and additional evaluation are required before others could safely build on the contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies an important systems problem and offers an intuitive, original perspective: predicting an output-length distribution and incorporating tail risk rather than relying only on a point estimate.
TIE is practically motivated and reasonably simple. It combines censored log-t predictions, adaptive CVaR weighting, starvation mitigation, and asynchronous batched prediction within vLLM.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: online and offline workloads, three datasets, Llama 8B/70B, and several additional dense and MoE models. TIE consistently improves the reported latency and throughput metrics, often substantially.

Useful ablations compare distribution families, expectation-only scheduling, fixed CVaR weights, and adaptive weighting. Cross-dataset and cross-model tests also provide encouraging evidence of generalization.

The manuscript is well organized and generally clear, with helpful diagrams, explicit derivations for censored expectation/CVaR, implementation discussion, and an honest acknowledgment that collecting repeated generations is costly.
weaknesses: The theoretical heavy-tail result is not established for general autoregressive decoding. The appendix replaces the step- and trajectory-dependent termination probabilities with a single, n-independent latent termination rate. This strong mixture-of-geometric assumption is neither implied by Assumption 3.1 as stated nor empirically validated; without it, Equation 17 and hence the theorem do not follow.

The goodness-of-fit evidence is statistically questionable. Ordinary KS p-values are not calibrated when distribution parameters are estimated from the tested samples, output lengths are discrete and capped, and the fixed degree of freedom is selected using the same data. Parametric bootstrap tests and held-out comparisons are needed before interpreting a 90.6% pass rate as strong support for the log-t model.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a systems paper. Essential generation and workload settings—temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, arrival process, run duration, seeds, and warm-up—are absent. Predictor optimization hyperparameters, train/validation splits, baseline configurations, and the precise Monte Carlo implementation are also insufficiently specified, while the text refers to code without providing an artifact.

Results appear to be single measurements without repetitions, confidence intervals, or variance estimates despite stochastic decoding. This is especially consequential because different scheduler runs may receive different sampled output lengths. It is unclear whether outputs or randomness were controlled across methods.

The comparison may conflate the TIE score with its systems implementation. TIE receives asynchronous dynamic-batched prediction, but the paper does not clearly establish that SSJF and LTR use the same prediction pipeline. An ablation separating distribution-aware scoring from asynchronous batching, plus oracle-length and matched-implementation baselines, is necessary.

The evaluation emphasizes heavily overloaded operation with extremely large TTFT values and does not report SLO attainment, goodput, fairness, maximum waiting time, or full-workload completion time. The fixed-horizon offline metrics inherently favor completing short requests and do not demonstrate that long requests avoid practically significant starvation.

The limitations and impact discussions are too narrow. They omit the statistical and deployment limitations above, the sensitivity to censoring and decoding policy, and privacy or governance considerations arising from training on LMSYS and ShareGPT user conversations. Overall, the idea is promising and the reported gains are encouraging, but the unsupported theorem and insufficiently controlled/reproducible evaluation currently outweigh the merits.

strengths: Soundness: The core intuition is compelling: output length is stochastic, and modeling a per-prompt distribution can provide useful scheduling information beyond a point prediction. Censoring at the maximum generation length is appropriately incorporated into the expectation and CVaR calculations.

Significance: Efficient LLM serving is important, and the reported gains are substantial: TIE improves latency and fixed-window completion counts across chatbot and synthetic-data-generation workloads, multiple datasets, and a broad set of dense and MoE models.

Originality: Combining prompt-conditioned log-t parameter prediction with a load-adaptive, tail-risk-aware scheduling score is a novel and practically simple contribution, even though it builds on classical stochastic scheduling and CVaR.

Evaluation: The paper includes useful distribution-family and score ablations, training-scale and temperature sensitivity studies, a preemptive baseline, robustness tests for scale-parameter errors, and cross-model/cross-dataset evaluations.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with informative diagrams, readable tables, derivations for the censored distribution, and an honest acknowledgment of the repeated-generation training-data requirement.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical heavy-tail result depends on a strong, unvalidated latent fixed-termination-rate mixture assumption. The effective rate is trajectory- and horizon-dependent, but the proof replaces it with a fixed random rate drawn at the start. Examples involving JSON or long-form writing do not establish the assumed density near zero, so describing the theorem as following from mild assumptions overstates its support.

Statistical methodology: The claimed log-t fit relies heavily on ordinary KS p-values after estimating distribution parameters from the same samples; these p-values are not calibrated without a parametric-bootstrap or Lilliefors-style correction. Outputs are also capped, yet the distribution-selection MLE appears to treat observations as uncensored. Both issues can inflate the reported 90.6–93.1% pass rates and undermine the empirical premise for choosing log-t.

Evaluation confounding: TIE includes asynchronous prediction, dynamic batching, and a particular DeBERTa predictor, but the manuscript does not clearly establish that SSJF and LTR receive the same scheduling infrastructure and prediction-resource treatment. The expectation-only TIE ablation already achieves 0.75 s/token versus 1.55–1.95 for LTR/SSJF, while adding adaptive CVaR improves this only to 0.67; thus most of the headline gain is not isolated as arising from tail-aware scoring.

Baseline coverage is insufficient to attribute gains to distribution modeling. There is no oracle SJF, calibrated quantile-regression or direct-CVaR predictor, ensemble uncertainty baseline, or point predictor using the same encoder, training protocol, and asynchronous scheduler. Comparing against these controls is necessary to separate distributional uncertainty from architecture, training, and systems effects.

The online experiments emphasize extremely overloaded regimes—at 100 RPS, average TTFT reaches tens to hundreds of seconds—without establishing stability, realistic admission control, or steady-state measurement windows. Average and P90 latency can improve by postponing long jobs; P99/max waiting time, slowdown, starvation frequency, and per-length fairness are not reported despite QoS and starvation claims.

The offline metrics are potentially misleading: time to the first 3,000 completions and completions within three minutes reward selecting intrinsically short outputs, so different schedulers complete different subsets of the 10,000 prompts. This does not demonstrate greater total-work throughput, and the paper does not measure total tokens/sec, makespan for a common request set, output quality, or selection bias in the completed samples.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as train/validation/test splitting, optimizer and training hyperparameters, random seeds and uncertainty intervals, exact generation and truncation settings, predictor hardware placement and resource accounting, workload arrival protocol, run duration/warm-up, and whether results are averaged across repetitions are absent or deferred to unspecified code.

Limitations and ethics are treated too narrowly. The discussion mentions repeated-generation data cost but not fairness/starvation risks, workload-shift calibration, biased completion subsets, or the privacy/licensing implications of LMSYS and ShareGPT data. The impact statement does not address how prioritizing predicted-short requests may systematically disadvantage particular users or task types.

strengths: Significance/originality: Modeling prompt-conditioned output length uncertainty and incorporating tail risk into LLM scheduling is a useful systems direction. TIE combines distribution prediction, CVaR-based prioritization, adaptive risk sensitivity, starvation decay, and asynchronous batched prediction in a practical vLLM implementation.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers online and offline settings, multiple datasets, 8B/70B models, seven additional model families, temperature shifts, training-scale sensitivity, prediction noise, and a preemptive baseline. Reported improvements are large and consistent across the tested configurations.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized; the scheduling pipeline, censoring motivation, implementation, and main ablations are easy to follow. The limitations section honestly identifies the substantial multi-generation training-data requirement.

Relevance and ethics: Improving inference efficiency is practically valuable and does not directly add harmful model capabilities. weaknesses: Soundness—theory: The heavy-tail theorem depends on replacing the trajectory- and horizon-dependent effective termination rate in Eq. 16 with a single fixed latent rate. This is a strong additional mixture-of-geometric assumption, not a consequence of autoregressive decoding or the stated density condition. The proof therefore does not establish that actual LLM output lengths are power-law or specifically log-t distributed.

Soundness—statistical testing: The reported KS p-values and pass rates use parameters estimated from the same samples, for which ordinary KS critical values are invalid without a parametric bootstrap or equivalent correction. Output lengths are also discrete and capped, while the fitted likelihood is continuous and apparently does not treat cap-reaching observations as censored. With only 100 generations per prompt, the tests have limited tail power. Consequently, the claimed 90.6–93.1% goodness-of-fit evidence is not reliable.

Soundness—causal attribution: The evaluation does not isolate distributional modeling from predictor capacity and systems engineering. TIE uses DeBERTa, specialized multi-pooling/heads, asynchronous dynamic batching, and a different training construction, whereas SSJF/LTR use different models and objectives. The paper lacks a matched DeBERTa point predictor, quantile/UCB baseline, oracle scheduler, and baseline implementations using the same queueing and prediction machinery. Notably, the paper's own SEPT ablation reaches 0.75 s/token versus TIE's 0.67, while LTR is 1.55; most of the headline 2.31x gain therefore cannot be attributed to CVaR or adaptive tail-risk handling.

Evaluation validity: Online experiments omit essential workload details such as run duration, warm-up, arrival process, seeds, repetitions, confidence intervals, and whether each offered RPS is below service capacity. TTFT values of hundreds of seconds suggest overloaded, growing queues, where results depend strongly on measurement horizon. Mean and P90 latency do not establish fairness for long jobs, and the starvation-decay mechanism is not evaluated using maximum waiting time, high-percentile slowdown, or per-length/prompt-group QoS.

The claimed offline “throughput” is the number of jobs completed within three minutes from a fixed 10K-job batch, while time@3K measures early completions. Reordering toward predicted-short jobs can improve both without improving total makespan, token throughput, or completed-work throughput. It can also bias the generated dataset toward prompts associated with short responses. Full-batch completion time, tokens/second, and output/prompt composition are needed before claiming a 1.42x throughput improvement.

The censored-CVaR presentation is internally incomplete. Equation 10 in the main text is only valid when alpha is below the continuous mass beneath the cap; Appendix B introduces a separate cap-atom case, but the paper does not state which branch the implementation uses. The appendix also incorrectly says the conditioning event has zero probability while defining CVaR with a greater-than-or-equal event: the censored distribution has positive mass at the cap. The resulting value happens to remain the cap, but the derivation and implementation specification need correction.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the extensive tables. Predictor optimization hyperparameters, train/validation/test splits, sampling settings beyond temperature, max-token values, random seeds, workload traces, predictor hardware placement/resource accounting, and baseline integration details are missing or deferred to unspecified code. The reported R-squared values lack a defined evaluation split, and possible overlap between LMSYS training, fitting, and workload prompts is not ruled out.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The paper discusses data-collection cost but not systematic deferral of long-form requests, differential predictor errors across languages or prompt classes, workload drift, privacy concerns in LMSYS/ShareGPT, or selection bias in partially completed SDG datasets. These issues are material because TIE explicitly trades service priority across users. Overall, the idea is promising, but the statistical foundation and experimental controls do not currently support the central performance and attribution claims.

strengths: The paper offers a useful and reasonably original perspective: output length is modeled as a prompt-conditioned distribution rather than a point estimate, and tail risk is incorporated through a censored expectation plus CVaR. This connects stochastic scheduling ideas to a practical LLM-serving problem.

The systems design is practical and well developed. Asynchronous prediction, dynamic batching, heap-based priority updates, and waiting-time decay address prediction overhead and starvation concerns, and the reported scheduling overhead is only 4.26 ms per request.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: online and offline workloads, three datasets, dense and MoE models, cross-model transfer, and comparison with FCFS, SSJF, LTR, and TRAIL. Reported improvements are substantial, including 2.31x lower average per-token latency than LTR at 100 RPS and 1.42x faster time-to-3K than LTR.

The ablations are informative. The paper studies distribution family, fixed versus dynamic degrees of freedom, expectation-only scheduling, fixed versus adaptive risk coefficients, training-data scale, sampling temperature, prediction noise, and preemptive scheduling.

Presentation is clear and polished, with a coherent progression from empirical motivation through modeling, implementation, and evaluation. The authors also acknowledge the important limitation that distribution fitting requires repeated generations per prompt; the impact statement raises no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The theoretical result does not establish heavy-tailed behavior for general autoregressive decoding. The appendix replaces the time-varying, trajectory-dependent EOS probabilities with a fixed latent termination rate and assumes its density has polynomial mass near zero. That assumption essentially builds in the power-law conclusion and is neither derived nor empirically tested. Moreover, the resulting power-law tail is asymptotically different from a log-t tail, weakening the claimed theoretical justification for the selected family.

The goodness-of-fit evidence is not statistically rigorous. KS p-values are reported after fitting distribution parameters on the same samples, for which ordinary KS critical values are generally invalid without a parametric bootstrap or an appropriate correction. The analysis also treats bounded, discrete token lengths using continuous distributions, and the distribution family and fixed degree of freedom appear selected on the same 1,000 prompts used to report fit quality.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate distributional scheduling from other design changes. TIE uses a different predictor architecture and introduces asynchronous batched prediction, while the manuscript describes prior prediction-based schedulers as synchronous. It is unclear whether every baseline received the same asynchronous runtime, batching policy, starvation mechanism, and comparable predictor capacity. A point-estimate baseline implemented within exactly the same infrastructure is needed; the expectation-only ablation helps but shows a much smaller gain than the headline comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly specify arrival-process generation, experiment duration and warm-up, random seeds, number of independent trials, variance or confidence intervals, maximum-generation limits, detailed train/validation/test splits, and many training hyperparameters. Several details are deferred to code, but no concrete artifact or availability statement is provided.

The chosen measurements leave important scheduling tradeoffs unresolved. At 100 RPS, average TTFT values of roughly 48–128 seconds suggest severe overload, making results sensitive to workload duration and accounting conventions. There are no P99/max completion-time, fairness, starvation, or slowdown results. The offline metric counts requests completed within a fixed window rather than token throughput, inherently favoring SJF-style policies and not establishing greater total computational throughput.

Claims that the fitted distribution captures uncertainty and generalizes across models would be stronger with direct held-out calibration metrics—such as quantile coverage, likelihood, CRPS, or tail calibration—on each target model and decoding configuration. Scheduling performance alone cannot determine whether gains arise from calibrated uncertainty, improved central length prediction, or implementation differences. Overall, the idea and results are promising enough for weak acceptance, but these evidential limitations reduce confidence in the strongest causal and theoretical claims.
